provenance: Questions in this file were adopted from the MIT-licensed project Onesayi/ccna-simulator at commit 6efca4f15e8ccf01fb44973b46bb26922797965a (Alistair Nhiwatiwa, 2026-10-04), originally authored against the CCNA v1.0 blueprint and re-keyed here to the v1.1 leaf objective IDs in src/data/objectives.json. The full per-question mapping, including every item dropped as out of scope and the reason, is in docs/ADOPTED.md. Each question records its origin in its `upstream` field. Distractor rationales are marked TODO and are written during Phase 2; no question ships without them.

questions.prompt: R1 learns 10.5.0.0/16 from both OSPF and EIGRP. Which route does it install, and why?

A.text: Whichever has the lower metric
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: The EIGRP route, because its administrative distance (90) is lower than OSPF’s (110)

D.text: The OSPF route, because its AD (110) is higher
D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: For the same prefix, the lowest AD wins. Metrics from different protocols are not comparable. Defaults: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.

questions.prompt: R1 learns 10.2.0.0/16 by OSPF over its primary link. You want a static route over a backup link that is used only if OSPF loses the route. What makes it a floating static?

A.text: Give it an administrative distance of 1
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.text: Give it a longer prefix, such as /24
B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.text: Give it an administrative distance above 110, for example 115

questions.explanation: With AD 115 the static loses to OSPF (110) while OSPF has the route and is installed only when it disappears. A longer prefix would always win.

questions.prompt: Two routers run HSRP with default settings. R1 was active, failed and has come back. Which router is active now?

A.text: R1, because HSRP preemption is on by default
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: R2 stays active, because HSRP preemption is off by default

D.text: R1, because it was active first
D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Without standby preempt, a recovered higher-priority router waits as standby. VRRP, by contrast, preempts by default.

questions.prompt:
R2# show standby brief
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       10   110 P Standby 10.1.1.2        local           10.1.1.254

What does this output from R2 tell you?

A.text: R2 is active for 10.1.1.254
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.text: R2 has priority 100 and preemption off
B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.text: R2 is standby with priority 110 and preempt on; 10.1.1.2 is active

questions.explanation: P means preempt. Since R2 has preempt and priority 110 but is still standby, the active router must have a higher priority (or a tie with a higher IP).

questions.prompt: The active HSRP router’s WAN link fails but it stays active, so traffic is black-holed. Which pair of settings fixes that?

D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Tracking drops the active router’s priority below its peer, and preempt lets the peer take over.

questions.prompt: Four routers share an Ethernet segment with default settings. How is the DR chosen?

A.text: The first router to boot, always
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.text: Highest interface priority, then highest router ID

C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Priority (default 1) decides first, then router ID. Priority 0 means never DR or BDR. The election is not preemptive once a DR exists.

questions.prompt: How does OSPF build its routing table?

A.text: Each router sends its full routing table to neighbors every 30 seconds
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.text: Routers trust the hop count their neighbors advertise
B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: A central controller pushes routes to every router
C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.text: Each router floods LSAs, builds the same link-state database and runs SPF (Dijkstra) on it

questions.explanation: OSPF is link state: everyone in the area shares a map and computes shortest paths. Periodic full tables are how distance-vector protocols like RIP work.
